extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature, philosophy, and writers interested in the nature of heroism and how to depict or recognize great men
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Carlyle's criteria for what makes a Hero (and how society should recognize and respond to Heroes); useful for literary criticism, creative-writing of heroic figures, and philosophical reflection on leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence for Excellence / Hero-worship
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine reverence for Excellence; a worship for Heroes (Bozzy's attitude toward Johnson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hero-worship is a natural and valuable human response: recognize and bend before true excellence. Carlyle treats this reverence as a social faculty that signals the presence of real greatness and is important to preserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadfastness / Brave endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading a difficult, confused existence wisely; 'led it well, like a right valiant man' with a 'loadstar' that guides action and refuses to strike the flag to the Spirit of Lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroes remain constant under adversity and disorganization: moral and practical steadfastness (Johnson as example: 'To the Spirit of Lies, bearing death and hunger, he would in nowise strike his flag').

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm, sustained Strength (not mere Vehemence)
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness is calm force for difficulty; strength means being able to 'walk under the heaviest weight without staggering' rather than spasmodic convulsions or intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish depth and width of force from mere intensity or vehemence (Rousseau is 'intense rather than strong'). The 'talent of Silence'—knowing when to hold peace until the right time—is an invaluable mark of strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Talent of Silence / Speaking with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero must often be able to 'hold his peace' until the time to speak and act; speech should be measured and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle praises speakers who 'spoke rather little than much' and 'always when he did speak, it was to throw new light on the matter' (Burns example). In writing/portrayal, favor concise, illuminating speech over constant outpouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnestness / Being 'in earnest'
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief characteristic of a Hero: he is heartily 'in earnest'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensity of conviction—actual commitment to truth or purpose—distinguishes genuine heroism; even flawed men can possess an ineradicable spark of 'heavenly fire' if truly earnest (Rousseau qualified by earnestness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-mastery and freedom from Egoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Victory over mere Desire; avoidance of Egoism, vanity, and hunger for praise which are the sources of faults and miseries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle contrasts greatness with Rousseau's 'Egoism'—a hero must not be driven by petty hunger for applause. In depiction, show restraint, inner discipline, and humility rather than craving for adulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and practical consequence of a Hero's message
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero's word, if true, must be believed and acted upon; heroes can be prophetic and can reshape society for good or evil depending upon their clarity and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle warns that disorganized or delirious heroism (Rousseau) can produce vast evil (e.g., revolutionary violence), while a true prophet (Johnson) accomplishes good even under disadvantage. Consider social effects when evaluating or writing heroic figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / Truthfulness in art and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and truth—'the song he sings is not of fantasticalities; it is of a thing felt, really there' (Burns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor 'white sunlight' (genuine insight) over 'rose-pink' operatic artificiality. Literary or heroic worth lies in being true to experience and reality rather than ornamented superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness, Simplicity, and Naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero often shows 'healthy robustness', homely, rustic honesty, and a combination of fiery passion with soft pity (Burns as 'noble rough genuineness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle admires straightforward, rooted character—strong but with wells of tenderness. In depiction, give heroes earthy strength and accessible humanity rather than polished artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful utterance / Insightful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that 'always has something in it'—utterances that are flashes of insight and worth remembering (shared trait of Burns and Mirabeau).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroes and great writers speak in ways that provide clear, memorable insight. In creative-writing, craft dialogue and aphorisms that illuminate rather than merely ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composure under sudden prosperity / humility in fame
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to meet sudden elevation or celebrity without being inflated or changed: 'he feels that _he_ there is the man Robert Burns; that the "rank is but the guinea-stamp;" ... the celebrity is but the candle-light'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray or expect heroes to retain identity and purpose when famous; losing oneself to 'Lionism' is a failure that can lead to moral and practical ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to admirers and career-cropping 'lion-hunters'
rubrics_metrics.description: External admirers can hinder a hero's work—'They gathered round him in his Farm; hindered his industry; ... the Hero's life went for it!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the destructive social dynamics of celebrity. Protect solitude, discipline, and the conditions of work; in narratives, show how adulation can be corrosive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingship as synthesis: the Able-man who commands
rubrics_metrics.description: The King/Able-man embodies summary of priest, teacher, commander—'the Commander over Men ... may be reckoned the most important of Great Men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruler should combine spiritual and practical guidance; in leadership portrayals, fuse moral authority, wisdom, and practical command rather than mere titular power.

rubrics_metrics.name: The social duty to find and invest the Able-man
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding the Ablest Man and investing him with symbols of ability is 'the business, well or ill accomplished, of all social procedure whatsoever'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society must seek true ability; systems that fail to elevate the capable produce disorder. For plots or worldbuilding, make selection of leadership a central, consequential process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral legitimacy of authority: 'Divine Right or Diabolic Wrong'
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim of rule/obedience contains either a divine (right) element or a diabolic (wrong) one; rule and obedience are moral acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority must have moral justification—either it is rightly sanctioned or it is a profound wrong. In criticism and fiction, interrogate the moral basis of power and obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideals must exist and be approximated
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals exist and although they cannot be fully embodied, approximations toward them are necessary; abandoning ideals leads to social ruin ('If they be not approximated to at all, the whole matter goes to wreck!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ideals as necessary guiding stars for individual and social life; in character arcs, show striving toward ideals even amid imperfect realization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Great Men even in revolutionary/egalitarian times
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a generation rejects authority ('Liberty and Equality') and claims 'no Authority needed any longer', the world still cannot do without Great Men—'we cannot do without Great Men!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting revolutions or egalitarian movements, account for the continuing human need for leadership and exemplary figures; hero-worship remains a 'polestar through smoke-clouds.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of placing unfit leaders at the head
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting a too 'Un_Able Man' or an ignoble, unvaliant, fatuous man in charge causes administrative failure and social explosion (bricks without plummet leading to collapse and Sansculottism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize selection and competence in governance narratives; demonstrate how misplacement of authority leads to predictable disaster and revolt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style criterion: depth and universality over second-hand prettiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary style that is 'operatic' or 'rose-pink' (superficial prettiness) is inferior to the 'True'—the depth and universal insight seen in Shakespeare, Goethe, Walter Scott.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer substantive, wide, and calm expression over fashionable or artificial affectations; in writing, aim for lasting universality rather than transient ornament.
